presenterNotes: Block 1: Use clear examples to distinguish mutually exclusive from non‑mutually exclusive. The Venn diagram visual is helpful.
Block 2: The formula is straightforward, but the subtraction is often forgotten. Drill multiple examples, both with and without overlap.
Block 3: Two‑way tables are a practical application. Have students practice identifying the correct cell for the intersection.
Block 4: Combining complement with Addition Rule is powerful. Introduce De Morgan's laws intuitively.
Block 5: The blueprint ties the section together. Emphasize the 'mutual exclusivity first' rule.

blocks.title: Mutually Exclusive Events
teacherCues: Ask: 'Can you roll a 3 and a 4 on a single die at the same time?' Then ask: 'Can you draw a king and a heart at the same time?'
Show a Venn diagram of two non‑overlapping circles versus overlapping circles.

explanation: Two events are [[kw:mutually exclusive]] if they [[imp:cannot occur at the same time]].
Mutually exclusive events have [[imp:no outcomes in common]]. In a Venn diagram, their circles do not overlap.
If events are not mutually exclusive, they can occur together (e.g., selecting a male and a nursing major).
For mutually exclusive events, $ P(A \text{ and } B) = 0 $.
Examples: Rolling a 3 and a 4 on one die (mutually exclusive); Selecting a heart and a king (not mutually exclusive).

discoveryHook.scenario: When you roll a die, getting a 3 and getting a 4 cannot happen together — they are mutually exclusive. But getting a heart and a king can happen together (the king of hearts). Recognizing whether events overlap is the first step in using the Addition Rule.

confusionCorner.body: Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together; independent events have no influence on each other's probability. In fact, mutually exclusive events with non‑zero probabilities are always [[imp:dependent]]: if one occurs, the other cannot. Keep these concepts separate!
confusionCorner.title: Mutually Exclusive ≠ Independent

discoveryHook.scenario: To find the probability that at least one of two events happens — a 4 or an ace, a heart or a king — we add their individual probabilities. But if they overlap, we've double‑counted the intersection, so we must subtract it. That's the Addition Rule.

formulaCard.title: Addition Rule Formulas
formulaCard.formula: $$P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B)$$ $$\text{If mutually exclusive: } P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B)$$

legend.meaning: probability of the intersection; subtracted to avoid double‑counting

rows.1: $ P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B) $

explanation: The [[kw:Addition Rule]] finds the probability that event $A$ or event $B$ (or both) occurs.
General formula: $ P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B) $.
If $A$ and $B$ are [[imp:mutually exclusive]], then $ P(A \text{ and } B) = 0 $, so the formula simplifies to $ P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) $.
The subtraction of $ P(A \text{ and } B) $ avoids double‑counting outcomes that belong to both events.
The word 'or' in probability is usually [[imp:inclusive]] (it includes the possibility of both).

confusionCorner.body: When events are not mutually exclusive, adding probabilities without subtracting the intersection will overstate the true probability. [[imp:Always check for overlap before applying the Addition Rule.]]
confusionCorner.title: Don't Forget to Subtract the Overlap!

blocks.title: The Addition Rule

discoveryHook.scenario: Real data often comes in two‑way tables — blood type and Rh‑factor, gender and charity involvement. The Addition Rule helps answer questions like 'What's the chance a donor has type O or is Rh‑positive?' directly from the table by summing the right cells and avoiding double‑counts.

blocks.title: Using the Addition Rule with Two‑Way Tables

legend.meaning: frequency from the appropriate row, column, or cell

explanation: Two‑way tables (contingency tables) show the joint frequencies of two categorical variables.
To use the Addition Rule with tables: find $P(A)$, $P(B)$, and $P(A \text{ and } B)$ from the cell counts and total.

$ P(A) = \frac{\text{total for row/column of } A}{n} $, $ P(B) = \frac{\text{total for row/column of } B}{n} $, $ P(A \text{ and } B) = \frac{\text{cell where } A \text{ and } B \text{ intersect}}{n} $.
Then apply $ P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B) $.
This method works whether events are mutually exclusive or not; if mutually exclusive, the intersection cell will be zero.

blocks.title: Combining the Addition Rule and Complements

confusionCorner.body: The complement of 'A or B' is 'not A and not B'. The complement of 'A and B' is 'not A or not B'. These are De Morgan's Laws. [[imp:Be careful when translating a 'not both' or 'neither' statement into an event.]]
confusionCorner.title: 'Or' vs. 'And' in Complements

visuals.title: Combining Rules for Draft Picks (256 picks)

explanation: The event 'not (A or B)' is the complement of 'A or B'.
So, $ P(\text{not } (A \text{ or } B)) = 1 - P(A \text{ or } B) $.
This is useful when finding the probability of avoiding multiple outcomes.
You can also use the complement to answer questions like 'probability that a person is not female or not involved in charity', which may require careful decomposition.

questions.prompt: In the blueprint, after solving, what is the final step? (Answer with one word.)
questions.feedbackIfWrong: The final step is Conclude — interpret the probability in context.

explanation: Blueprint steps: [[imp:Understand → Solve → Conclude]].
1. [[kw:Understand]]: Define events $A$ and $B$. Determine whether they are mutually exclusive (can they occur together?). Identify total sample space.

2. [[kw:Solve]]: Compute $P(A)$, $P(B)$, and $P(A \text{ and } B)$ from counts, table, or given probabilities. Apply the Addition Rule: $P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B)$. If mutually exclusive, omit the subtraction.
3. [[kw:Conclude]]: Calculate the probability. If the question involves 'not', use the complement. Interpret the result in context, checking for unusual events ($P \leq 0.05$).

legend.meaning: Check mutual exclusivity first — it determines the formula.

formulaCard.title: Blueprint Decision Tree
formulaCard.formula: $$\text{'Or' Problem} \;\begin{cases} \text{Mutually exclusive?} & \;\begin{cases} \text{Yes} & \;\rightarrow\; P(A)+P(B) \\ \text{No} & \;\rightarrow\; P(A)+P(B)-P(A \text{ and } B) \end{cases} \\ \text{Want 'not'?} & \;\rightarrow\; 1 - P(\text{event}) \end{cases}$$

rows.2: Can A and B happen together?

rows.1: Add, then subtract intersection: $P(A)+P(B)-P(A \text{ and } B)$

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid: Solving 'Or' Probability Problems

confusionCorner.body: Skipping the mutual exclusivity check is the most common mistake with the Addition Rule. Even a tiny overlap changes the answer. [[imp:Make it the first question you ask: 'Can these events both happen?' If yes, subtract.]]
confusionCorner.title: Always Check the Overlap

discoveryHook.scenario: Facing a probability problem with the word 'or'? The blueprint gives you a clear path: identify the events, check if they can both occur, apply the Addition Rule (with or without subtraction), and interpret the result. No more guessing!
